# Pityriasis versicolor

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Pediatrics > Pediatric dermatology > Pityriasis versicolor*

[Original Article Link](/library/Zk0ZmT)

---

## Summary

Pityriasis versicolor is a benign, <u>superficial fungal infection</u> most commonly caused by <u>Malassezia furfur</u> or <u>Malassezia globosa</u>. Although the condition occurs worldwide, the <u>incidence</u> is higher in tropical climates. It typically manifests as a well-demarcated, <u>macular rash</u> with round or oval <u>hyperpigmented</u>, <u>hypopigmented</u>, or <u>erythematous</u> lesions that often coalesce. The seborrheic areas of the upper trunk and neck are primarily affected, and the lesions are more noticeable after UV exposure because the surrounding <u>skin</u> darkens while the affected <u>skin</u> does not. Pityriasis versicolor is usually a <u>clinical diagnosis</u>; however, <u>potassium hydroxide (KOH) microscopy</u> of <u>skin</u> scrapings that show <u>hyphae</u> and spores in a characteristic “spaghetti-and-meatballs” pattern confirms the diagnosis. Topical drugs such as <u>selenium</u> sulfide and <u>ketoconazole</u> are recommended for initial treatment; systemic therapy is reserved for extensive or refractory disease. Lesions will resolve completely over time, but recurrences are common.




Pityriasis versicolor was previously known as <u>tinea</u> versicolor, as it was believed to be a <u>dermatophyte infection</u>. Some sources still refer to the condition by its original name.

---

## Epidemiology

* Occurs worldwide, with a higher <u>incidence</u> in tropical climates

* More prevalent in healthy individuals 21–30 years of age [[1]](/library/BQbzyt)




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

### Pathogens




* Malassezia spp. (previously known as Pityrosporum): most commonly Malassezia globosa and Malassezia furfur

* Dimorphic, <u>lipophilic</u> <u>yeast</u>-like fungi that are part of the <u>normal skin flora</u>

* Not contagious





### <u>Risk factors</u>




* Hot and humid climates  [[2]](/library/gF0Fh3)[[3]](/library/9QbNyt)

* <u>Excessive sweating</u>, <u>seborrhea</u>, and oily <u>skin</u>

* <u>Immunosuppression</u>

* <u>Cushing syndrome</u>

* Genetic predisposition

---

## Pathophysiology

* Malassezia spp. infect the stratum corneum → lipid degradation → production of acids that inhibit <u>tyrosinase</u> and damage <u>melanocytes</u> → <u>hypopigmentation</u>

* Inflammatory response to pathogens → <u>hyperpigmentation</u>

---

## Clinical features

* Symmetrically affects the seborrheic areas of the upper trunk (chest, shoulders, upper arms) and neck  [[4]](/library/Bedza60)

* In children: Facial involvement is also common.

* <u>Immunocompromised individuals</u>: Extensive disease may be seen.

* <u>Rash</u> appears as round or oval <u>macules</u> 1–3 cm in diameter [[5]](/library/SSWy_k0)

* Lesions often coalesce into well-demarcated irregular patches. [[4]](/library/Bedza60)

* Color of the lesions may vary in the affected individual (i.e., <u>hypopigmented</u>, <u>hyperpigmented</u>, <u>erythematous</u>) ;  [[4]](/library/Bedza60)

* Lesions may change color with seasons (e.g., lighter than surrounding <u>skin</u> during summer, darker than surrounding <u>skin</u> in winter).

* <u>Hypopigmentation</u> is typical in individuals with darker <u>skin</u>. [[6]](/library/QqduyI0)

* May be mildly pruritic [[4]](/library/Bedza60)[[7]](/library/rIdfVr0)

* Fine, bran-like, subtle <u>scaling</u> if the <u>skin</u> is stretched or gently scraped (evoked scale sign) [[4]](/library/Bedza60)[[6]](/library/QqduyI0)[[8]](/library/7Id4Vr0)





> [!TIP]
> Lesions are more noticeable after UV exposure because the surrounding <u>skin</u> darkens while the affected <u>skin</u> does not. [[4]](/library/Bedza60)

## Diagnosis

* Diagnosis is usually clinical. [[4]](/library/Bedza60)[[9]](/library/XPW9Wl0)

* <u>Wood lamp examination</u> can support the diagnosis; affected areas fluoresce yellow-green. [[4]](/library/Bedza60)[[5]](/library/SSWy_k0)

* <u>KOH microscopy</u> confirms the diagnosis. [[4]](/library/Bedza60)[[9]](/library/XPW9Wl0)

* Sample <u>skin</u> scrapings of the affected area.

* Findings: <u>hyphae</u> and spores arranged in a “spaghetti-and-meatballs” pattern





> [!TIP]
> A fungal culture is usually not performed as the <u>yeast</u> can be part of <u>normal skin flora</u>. [[4]](/library/Bedza60)




![Malassezia furfur](media/nc0x7al1cpctzoinfbcie4iz.jpg)

Malassezia furfur

---

## Differential diagnoses

* <u>Vitiligo</u>

* <u>Seborrheic dermatitis</u>

* <u>Pityriasis rosea</u>

* <u>Pityriasis alba</u>

* <u>Guttate psoriasis</u>

* <u>Erythrasma</u>

* <u>Mycosis fungoides</u>

* Pityrosporum folliculitis: an infection of <u>hair follicles</u> caused by Malassezia spp. that typically manifests as pruritic, <u>papulopustular</u> eruptions. [[2]](/library/gF0Fh3)[[10]](/library/N40-jT)

* Usually occurs in <u>immunocompromised</u> patients (e.g., <u>HIV</u>, <u>immunosuppressive therapy</u>, <u>stress</u>, <u>diabetes</u>, <u>steroid</u> therapy)

* Often difficult to distinguish from <u>acne vulgaris</u> (and may also occur concurrently with it)




The differential diagnoses listed here are not exhaustive.

---

## Treatment

### Localized disease [[4]](/library/Bedza60)[[5]](/library/SSWy_k0)




* First-line: topical therapy

* Options include:   [[4]](/library/Bedza60)[[5]](/library/SSWy_k0)[[7]](/library/rIdfVr0)

* <u>Azoles</u>: <u>clotrimazole</u> DOSAGE, <u>ketoconazole</u> (<u>off-label</u> in children aged < 12 years) DOSAGE [[4]](/library/Bedza60)[[5]](/library/SSWy_k0)

* <u>Selenium</u> sulfide (<u>off-label</u> in children aged < 12 years) DOSAGE [[4]](/library/Bedza60)[[5]](/library/SSWy_k0)

* <u>Zinc</u> pyrithione (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[11]](/library/HIdKVr0)

* <u>Terbinafine</u> (<u>off-label</u> in children) DOSAGE [[4]](/library/Bedza60)

* Discoloration may take months to resolve; signs of treatment response include: [[4]](/library/Bedza60)

* Disappearance of scale

* Absence of “spaghetti-and-meatball” appearance on <u>KOH preparation</u>

* Recurrences are common; consider once-weekly or once-monthly prophylactic topical therapy (<u>off-label</u>). [[4]](/library/Bedza60)





### Extensive or refractory disease [[4]](/library/Bedza60)[[5]](/library/SSWy_k0)




* Consider systemic therapy; consult specialists for pediatric dosages.

* Preferred: <u>fluconazole</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[4]](/library/Bedza60)[[5]](/library/SSWy_k0)

* Alternative: <u>itraconazole</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[4]](/library/Bedza60)





> [!TIP]
> Systemic <u>griseofulvin</u> and <u>terbinafine</u> are not effective in treating pityriasis versicolor. [[5]](/library/SSWy_k0)
